questions.prompt: What does `lst[::-1]` produce for `lst = [1, 2, 3]`?
choices: A new list, reversed
The same list object, mutated in place
A ValueError
Only the first and last elements

query.title: Extended slicing: `seq[start:stop:step]`
query.explanation: A negative step walks the sequence backward. Omitting start and stop with a step of -1 tells Python to walk the entire sequence from end to start, and slicing always returns a new list rather than mutating the original. This is distinct from `.reverse()`, which mutates the list in place and returns `None`.

questions.prompt: What happens when you evaluate `i` immediately after `y = [i for i in range(3)]` in Python 3?
questions.code:
y = [i for i in range(3)]
print(i)
choices: Prints `2`
Prints `3`
Raises `NameError`
Prints `0`

query.title: Comprehension scoping
query.explanation: Unlike a `for` loop, a list/set/dict comprehension runs in its own implicit function scope in Python 3. The loop variable does not leak into the enclosing scope, so referencing `i` afterward raises `NameError`. Python 2 leaked the variable; this is one of the behavior changes between the two.

questions.prompt: A closure created inside a loop captures the loop variable by reference, so every lambda in `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` returns `2` when called after the loop finishes.

query.title: Late-binding closures
query.syntax: lambda: i   # captures the variable, not its value
query.explanation: Python closures bind to the variable itself, not its value at definition time. By the time any of the lambdas are called, the loop has finished and `i` holds its final value. The standard fix is to bind the current value as a default argument: `lambda i=i: i`.

questions.prompt: Inside a function signature, `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a:
choices: dict
list
tuple
set

query.title: Variadic positional parameters
query.explanation: The single-star form packs remaining positional arguments into a `tuple`, which is immutable and preserves call order. The double-star form (`**kwargs`) packs remaining keyword arguments into a `dict`. Mixing the two forms is common for wrapper functions that forward a call unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which dunder method is invoked when Python enters a `with obj:` block?
choices: __init__
__call__
__enter__
__context__

query.title: The context manager protocol
query.syntax:
__enter__(self) -> Any
__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb) -> bool | None
query.explanation: `__enter__` runs when the `with` block is entered and its return value is bound to the `as` target. `__exit__` always runs on exit, exception or not, and receives the exception info as three arguments. Returning a truthy value from `__exit__` suppresses the exception instead of letting it propagate.

questions.prompt: What are `bool([])` and `bool([0])`, respectively?
choices: False, False
True, True
False, True
True, False

query.title: Truthiness of containers
query.explanation: Containers are falsy only when they are empty. `[]` has length zero and is falsy. `[0]` has one element, and the element being the falsy integer `0` is irrelevant, the container itself is non-empty and therefore truthy.

questions.prompt: In `def f(x=[]): x.append(1); return x`, every call to `f()` with no argument shares and mutates the same default list object.

query.title: The mutable default argument trap
query.syntax: def f(x=[]): ...   # evaluated once, at def time
query.explanation: Default argument values are evaluated exactly once, when the function is defined, and stored on the function object. A mutable default like `[]` is therefore the same object across every call that omits the argument, and mutations accumulate. The idiomatic fix is `def f(x=None): x = [] if x is None else x`.

questions.prompt: What must the argument to `'-'.join(...)` be?
choices: A single string
Any iterable of strings
A list of any type
A dictionary

query.title: str.join(iterable)
query.explanation: `join` is a method on the separator string, not on the collection, which trips up people coming from languages where it hangs off the list. It accepts any iterable, not just a list, but every element must already be a `str`; joining a list containing an `int` raises `TypeError`.

questions.prompt: Inside a function signature, `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a:
choices: tuple
list
dict
namedtuple

query.title: Variadic keyword parameters
query.explanation: Every keyword argument not matched by an explicit parameter is collected into a regular `dict`, keyed by the argument name as a string, in the order the caller supplied them (dict ordering is insertion order as of Python 3.7).

questions.prompt: What does `"{:.2f}".format(3.14159)` evaluate to?

query.title: Format specification mini-language
query.explanation: The `.2f` spec means fixed-point notation with two digits after the decimal point, rounding rather than truncating. The same mini-language works inside f-strings (`f'{value:.2f}'`) and with the built-in `format()` function.

questions.prompt: What does calling a function defined with `yield` in its body return, before any iteration happens?
questions.code:
def counter():
    yield 1
    yield 2

result = counter()
choices: A generator object; the body has not run yet
The value `1`, immediately
A list `[1, 2]`
A `TypeError`, because `yield` requires `return` too

query.title: Generator functions are lazy
query.explanation: Any function containing a `yield` statement is a generator function. Calling it does not execute any of the body; it immediately returns a generator object. Code in the body only runs incrementally as the generator is advanced with `next()` or a `for` loop.

questions.prompt: A generator expression `(x * 2 for x in range(1000000))` builds the entire sequence in memory immediately, the same way `[x * 2 for x in range(1000000)]` does.

query.title: Generator expressions vs list comprehensions
query.syntax:
(expr for target in iterable)   # lazy
[expr for target in iterable]   # eager
query.explanation: Parentheses instead of brackets produce a generator expression, which yields items one at a time on demand and never materializes the full sequence. The bracketed form builds and stores every element in a list up front, so it uses memory proportional to the input size while the generator form uses constant memory.

questions.prompt: What is `logger` in the following snippet, once the module has finished loading?
choices: The original `greet` function, unchanged
Whatever object `log(greet)` returned, rebound to the name `greet`
A syntax error, decorators cannot take user-defined functions
Both `log` and `greet` merged into one function object

query.title: Decorators are just function application
query.explanation: The `@decorator` line above a function definition is pure syntax sugar for calling the decorator with the function and rebinding the name to whatever it returns. If the decorator returns a different callable (commonly a wrapper), every future call to `greet` actually invokes that wrapper instead of the original body.

questions.prompt: Why do well-written decorators apply `functools.wraps(fn)` to their inner wrapper?
choices: It makes the wrapper run faster
It copies `__name__`, `__doc__`, and other metadata from the original function onto the wrapper
It is required for the decorator syntax to work at all
It prevents the wrapper from accepting keyword arguments

query.title: functools.wraps
query.explanation: Without `functools.wraps`, the returned wrapper function has its own generic `__name__` (`"wrapper"`) and loses the original docstring, which breaks introspection tools, help(), and debuggers. `functools.wraps` copies that metadata across so the decorated function still looks like itself from the outside.

questions.prompt: Given `nums = [1, 2, 3]`, calling `print(*nums)` unpacks the list so each element becomes a separate positional argument, printing `1 2 3` rather than the list `[1, 2, 3]`.

query.title: Unpacking an iterable at a call site
query.syntax: f(*iterable)   # each element becomes a separate positional argument
query.explanation: The single-star prefix at a call site, not a function definition, unpacks an iterable so each of its elements becomes a separate positional argument. `print(*nums)` is therefore equivalent to `print(1, 2, 3)`, which joins the arguments with a space by default rather than printing the list representation.

questions.prompt: What does `f(**opts)` do at a call site, given `opts = {"sep": "-", "end": "!"}`?
choices: Raises `TypeError` because dicts cannot be passed to functions
Passes the dict itself as one positional argument
Expands the dict into keyword arguments `sep='-', end='!'`
Passes only the dict’s keys as positional arguments

query.title: Unpacking a dict into keyword arguments
query.syntax: f(**mapping)   # each key becomes a keyword argument name
query.explanation: The double-star prefix at a call site expands a mapping so each key/value pair becomes a keyword argument, matched by name against the callee’s parameters. Here it is equivalent to writing `print("a", "b", sep="-", end="!")` directly; every key must be a valid parameter name or the call raises `TypeError`.

questions.prompt: What gets embedded in the resulting string for `f"{name.upper()}"` if `name = "ana"`?
choices: The literal text 'name.upper()'
'ANA'
A `SyntaxError`, method calls are not allowed inside f-strings
'ana'

query.title: f-strings evaluate arbitrary expressions
query.explanation: Anything inside the curly braces of an f-string is evaluated as a normal Python expression at run time, not just a bare variable name. That means attribute access, method calls, indexing, and even function calls are all valid, and the string interpolates whatever that expression returns.

questions.prompt: What does the `=` specifier do in an f-string like `f"{count=}"`?
choices: It is a syntax error in f-strings
It prints just the value: '5'
It prints both the expression text and its value: 'count=5'
It assigns 5 to a new variable called count

query.title: Self-documenting f-strings
query.explanation: Added in Python 3.8, a trailing `=` inside an f-string replacement field prints the source text of the expression, an equals sign, and then the evaluated `repr()` of its value. It is a debugging convenience so you do not have to type `f"count={count}"` by hand.

questions.prompt: What does `{k: len(k) for k in ["a", "bb", "ccc"]}` evaluate to?
choices: A SyntaxError, dict comprehensions need two `for` clauses

query.title: Dict comprehensions
query.explanation: A dict comprehension mirrors a list comprehension but produces key/value pairs instead of single values, separated by a colon. Each iteration of the loop computes both the key expression and the value expression and inserts that pair into the resulting dict, later keys overwriting earlier ones if they collide.

questions.prompt: Writing `{}` as a literal on its own creates an empty `set`, not an empty `dict`.

query.title: Empty `{}` is a dict, not a set
query.explanation: Curly braces are ambiguous between dicts and sets, but Python resolves an empty pair of braces as an empty dict for historical reasons, `{}` predates set literals. To get an empty set you must call `set()` explicitly; a set comprehension like `{x for x in ...}` is unambiguous because it has no colon.

questions.prompt: What does `with open("a") as fa, open("b") as fb:` do?
questions.code:
with open("a") as fa, open("b") as fb:
    data = fa.read() + fb.read()
choices: Only opens the first file, the second is ignored
Opens both files, entering two context managers in one `with` statement
Raises a `SyntaxError`, `with` only accepts one context manager
Opens the files sequentially, closing `fa` before opening `fb`

query.title: Multiple context managers in one `with`
query.syntax:
with cm1() as a, cm2() as b:
    ...
query.explanation: A single `with` statement can list several context managers separated by commas. They are entered left to right and, crucially, exited right to left in reverse order even if an exception occurs partway through the block, guaranteeing both resources get cleaned up.

questions.prompt: What does `@contextlib.contextmanager` let you write a context manager as?
choices: A class implementing `__enter__` and `__exit__`
A generator function with exactly one `yield`, split into setup and teardown code
A lambda that returns a tuple of two functions
A regular function that must call `return` twice

query.title: contextlib.contextmanager
query.explanation: The decorator turns a generator function into a context manager without writing a class. Code before the `yield` runs as `__enter__`, the yielded value becomes the `as` target, and code after the `yield` runs as `__exit__`, including on the resumed line if an exception is thrown into the generator.

questions.prompt: Writing `raise ValueError("bad") from original_exc` links `original_exc` as the new exception’s `__cause__`, and it appears in the traceback.

query.title: Exception chaining
query.explanation: The `from` clause explicitly sets the `__cause__` attribute on the exception being raised, and the traceback printer shows both exceptions with a note that the first was the direct cause of the second. Without an explicit `from`, Python still records an implicit `__context__` when one exception is raised while handling another.

questions.prompt: What is the idiomatic way to define a custom exception type in Python?
choices: Subclass `Exception` (or a more specific built-in exception)
Subclass `dict`, since exceptions are just structured data
Decorate a plain function with `@exception`
There is no way to add custom fields to an exception

query.title: Custom exception classes
query.explanation: Custom exceptions subclass `Exception` or one of its more specific built-in descendants so they integrate with `try`/`except` matching by type. Storing extra data as instance attributes, as `self.balance` does here, lets calling code inspect the failure programmatically instead of parsing the message string.

questions.prompt: What does declaring `radius` as a `@property` let callers do?
choices: Call it like `c.radius()`
Access it like a plain attribute, `c.radius`, while it actually runs a method
Nothing, `@property` only works on class-level constants
Access it as `Circle.radius` without an instance

query.title: @property
query.explanation: `@property` turns a method into a descriptor so that accessing `instance.radius` runs the decorated method automatically and returns its result, with no parentheses at the call site. This lets a class expose what looks like a plain attribute while still computing or validating the value on every access.

questions.prompt: What is required to make `c.radius = 5` work for the `radius` property below?
choices: Nothing extra, every `@property` is automatically settable
A separate method decorated with `@radius.setter`, using the same method name
Overriding `__setattr__` on the class
Making `radius` a class variable instead of a property

query.title: Property setters
query.explanation: A bare `@property` is read-only by default; assigning to it raises `AttributeError`. Adding a method decorated with `@radius.setter`, sharing the property’s name, wires up the assignment path so `instance.radius = value` calls that method, which is exactly where validation logic like the range check here belongs.

questions.prompt: A method decorated with `@staticmethod` automatically receives `self` as its first argument, just like a normal instance method.

query.title: @staticmethod
query.explanation: A static method does not receive `self` or `cls` automatically; it is just a regular function that happens to live inside the class’s namespace for organizational purposes. It cannot access instance state or class state unless those are passed in explicitly as arguments.

questions.prompt: Why do factory constructors like `dict.fromkeys` use `@classmethod`?
choices: It gives the method access to the class itself via `cls`, so it can call `cls(...)` and work correctly for subclasses too
It is required syntax for any method that returns an instance
It makes the method private
`cls` is just a naming convention with no special behavior

query.title: @classmethod as alternate constructor
query.explanation: A classmethod receives the class itself, conventionally named `cls`, as its first argument instead of an instance. Using `cls(...)` instead of hardcoding `Pizza(...)` means the alternate constructor keeps working correctly if a subclass inherits it, since `cls` refers to whichever class the method was actually called through.

questions.prompt: Calling `enumerate(["a", "b"], start=1)` begins counting from `1` instead of `0`, without changing which value is paired with which item.

query.title: enumerate() with a custom start
query.explanation: By default `enumerate` pairs each element with an index starting at 0, but the `start` keyword shifts where counting begins without changing which elements are paired with which position. Each pair is a two-tuple `(index, value)`, commonly unpacked in a `for index, value in enumerate(...)` loop.

questions.prompt: `list(zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"]))` produces three pairs, padding the shorter list with `None`.

query.title: zip() truncates to the shortest iterable
query.explanation: `zip` stops as soon as any of its input iterables is exhausted, it never pads. Here the second list has only two elements, so the result has exactly two pairs and the extra `3` from the first list is silently dropped. Use `itertools.zip_longest` if padding with a fill value is what you actually want.

questions.prompt: How do you sort a list of strings by length instead of alphabetically?
choices: sorted(words, compare=len)
sorted(words, key=len)
words.sort(len)
sorted(words, by=len)

query.title: sorted(..., key=...)
query.explanation: The `key` argument takes a one-argument function applied to each element to compute the value actually used for comparison, without changing what gets returned. Python computes each key once per element up front rather than recomputing it repeatedly during comparisons, which is why it is usually faster than a hand-written comparator.

questions.prompt: What does `sorted([3, 1, 2], reverse=True)` return?

query.title: sorted(..., reverse=True)
query.explanation: Setting `reverse=True` sorts in descending order directly, it is not the same as sorting ascending and then reversing the list, though the two happen to produce the same result for a simple total order like integers. It composes with `key=` too, applying the reversal after keys are computed.

questions.prompt: What does `collections.Counter("mississippi")` let you get easily?
questions.code:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter("mississippi")
c["s"]
choices: The index of the first "s"
The number of times "s" appears in the string
A boolean for whether "s" is in the string
A `KeyError`, `Counter` only works on lists

query.title: collections.Counter
query.syntax: Counter(iterable)   # dict subclass mapping element -> count
query.explanation: `Counter` is a `dict` subclass that tallies how many times each hashable element appears in the iterable it is built from. Unlike a plain dict, looking up a missing key returns `0` instead of raising `KeyError`, and it comes with helpers like `.most_common(n)` for ranked frequency reports.

questions.prompt: What problem does `collections.defaultdict(list)` solve compared to a plain dict?
questions.code:
from collections import defaultdict
groups = defaultdict(list)
groups["a"].append(1)
choices: It sorts keys automatically
It avoids a `KeyError` by auto-creating a new list the first time a key is accessed
It makes the dict immutable
It limits the dict to a fixed maximum size

query.title: collections.defaultdict
query.syntax: defaultdict(factory)   # factory() builds a missing value
query.explanation: A `defaultdict` is constructed with a zero-argument factory function. The first time a missing key is looked up, instead of raising `KeyError` it calls the factory, stores the result under that key, and returns it, which is exactly what a "group items by key" pattern needs without a manual `if key not in dict` check.

questions.prompt: What can you do with a `collections.namedtuple` that you cannot do with a plain tuple?
questions.code:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x", "y"])
p = Point(1, 2)
p.x
choices: Mutate its fields after creation
Access fields by name (`p.x`) in addition to by index (`p[0]`)
Store more than 255 elements
Nest it inside a dict, which plain tuples cannot do

query.title: collections.namedtuple
query.explanation: `namedtuple` generates a lightweight, immutable class that behaves exactly like a tuple, supporting indexing and unpacking, while also exposing each position as a named attribute. This makes code that reads `p.x` and `p.y` far more self-documenting than the equivalent `p[0]` and `p[1]`, with no extra memory overhead per instance.

questions.prompt: What does `list(itertools.chain([1, 2], [3, 4], [5]))` produce?
choices: A TypeError, chain needs a single iterable of iterables

query.title: itertools.chain
query.explanation: `itertools.chain` takes any number of iterables and returns a single lazy iterator that yields every element of the first, then every element of the second, and so on, without first concatenating them into one combined list in memory. It is the idiomatic replacement for repeated list `+` concatenation when you only need to iterate once.

questions.prompt: What does `list(itertools.combinations([1, 2, 3], 2))` produce?

query.title: itertools.combinations
query.explanation: `combinations` returns every possible way to choose `r` elements from the iterable without regard to order and without repeating an element, so `(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)` count as the same combination and only one appears. Contrast with `itertools.permutations`, which treats order as significant and would include both.

questions.prompt: For `original = {"a": [1, 2]}`, `copy.copy(original)` produces a new dict, but `shallow["a"]` is still the exact same list object as `original["a"]`.

query.title: Shallow copy vs deep copy
query.explanation: `copy.copy` creates a new outer container but only copies references to the nested objects it contains, so mutating the shared inner list through either name affects both. `copy.deepcopy` walks the entire structure recursively and creates independent copies of every nested mutable object, which is slower but avoids this aliasing.

questions.prompt: If a class defines `__repr__` but not `__str__`, what does `str(instance)` use?
choices: Python's default `<Point object at 0x...>` text, ignoring `__repr__`
It falls back to `__repr__`
It raises `AttributeError`
It returns an empty string

query.title: __repr__ as the fallback for __str__
query.syntax:
__repr__(self) -> str   # unambiguous, for developers
__str__(self) -> str    # readable, for end users
query.explanation: When `__str__` is not defined, `str()` and `print()` fall back to whatever `__repr__` returns. The convention is that `__repr__` should be unambiguous enough to (ideally) recreate the object, while `__str__`, when defined separately, is a friendlier, human-facing description; the interactive interpreter always shows `__repr__` directly.

questions.prompt: Without overriding `__eq__`, two instances of a plain custom class that hold identical attribute values will compare equal with `==`.

query.title: Default equality is identity
query.syntax:
def __eq__(self, other):
    return isinstance(other, Point) and self.x == other.x
query.explanation: Without an overridden `__eq__`, a class inherits `object.__eq__`, which considers two instances equal only if they are literally the same object in memory. So `Point(1) == Point(1)` is `False` even though both hold `x = 1`, because they are two distinct instances; defining `__eq__` is what lets `==` compare by value instead.

questions.prompt: What does `@functools.total_ordering` do once a class defines `__eq__` and one ordering method like `__lt__`?
choices: It fills in the remaining comparisons (`__le__`, `__gt__`, `__ge__`) automatically
It requires you to still define all six comparison methods yourself
It makes the class sortable without defining any comparison method
It overrides `__eq__` to always return `True`

query.title: functools.total_ordering
query.explanation: Implementing all six rich comparison dunders by hand is repetitive, so `total_ordering` derives the rest from just `__eq__` plus one of `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__`, or `__ge__`. It saves boilerplate at a small runtime cost compared to defining every method directly, since the derived methods dispatch through the one you wrote.

questions.prompt: Given `a, *b, c = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, what are `a`, `b`, and `c`?
choices: a=1, b=[2, 3, 4, 5], c=undefined
A ValueError, only one starred target is allowed and it must be last

query.title: Extended (starred) unpacking
query.explanation: Exactly one target in an unpacking assignment may be prefixed with `*`, and it absorbs every element not claimed by the other, fixed-position targets, always as a list. Here `a` takes the first element, `c` takes the last, and `b` collects everything in between, regardless of the sequence’s total length.

questions.prompt: What does the walrus operator accomplish inside this comprehension that a plain condition could not do without recomputing?
questions.code:
data = ["1", "x", "3"]
results = [n for s in data if (n := int(s)) if False]  # illustrative
valid = [y for x in data if (y := safe_parse(x)) is not None]
choices: It filters on the parsed value while reusing it as the output, without calling the parser twice
It declares `y` as a global variable
It is only legal inside `while` loops, not comprehensions
It converts the comprehension into a generator expression automatically

query.title: Walrus operator inside a comprehension filter
query.syntax: [y for x in it if (y := transform(x)) condition]
query.explanation: Using `:=` in the `if` clause of a comprehension lets you compute a value once, bind it to a name, test that name in the same condition, and reuse the bound name as the output expression. Without it you would either call `transform(x)` twice (once to filter, once to produce the result) or fall back to a full `for` loop.

questions.prompt: Adding a type hint like `def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:` makes Python raise a `TypeError` at call time if you pass in strings instead.

query.title: Type hints are not enforced at runtime
query.explanation: Function annotations are purely advisory as far as the interpreter is concerned; CPython never checks them when the function is called. They exist for static type checkers like mypy or pyright, IDEs, and documentation, catching mismatches before the code even runs rather than raising anything themselves at run time.

questions.prompt: What does the type hint `Optional[str]` mean?
choices: The parameter is optional and can be omitted from the call
It is shorthand for `Union[str, None]`, the value is either a `str` or `None`
It means the function returns nothing
It marks the function as deprecated

query.title: typing.Optional
query.explanation: `Optional[str]` does not describe an optional function argument, despite the name; it describes a value whose type is either `str` or `None`. It is purely a readability shorthand for `Union[str, None]` and is checked, like all type hints, by an external static checker rather than by the interpreter.

questions.prompt: Running Python with the `-O` optimization flag can cause `assert` statements to be skipped entirely, so code should never rely on `assert` for security checks.

query.title: assert can be optimized away
query.explanation: When Python runs with `-O` (or `PYTHONOPTIMIZE` set), the compiler strips `assert` statements from the bytecode entirely as a performance optimization, along with `__debug__` blocks. Because the check can simply vanish depending on how the interpreter was invoked, `assert` is meant for debugging invariants, not for validating untrusted input or enforcing security rules.

questions.prompt: Why does this function fail to update the module-level counter as intended?
choices: It does not fail, `count` updates correctly
Assigning to `count` anywhere in the function makes Python treat it as a local, so reading it before the assignment raises `UnboundLocalError`
Module-level variables can never be read inside a function
`count + 1` is invalid syntax

query.title: The global keyword
query.explanation: Python decides at compile time whether a name inside a function is local or not by scanning the whole function body; any assignment target makes that name local for the entire function, even on lines before the assignment. To actually reassign the module-level `count`, the function needs `global count` declared before it is used, telling Python not to treat it as local.

questions.prompt: What does `nonlocal` do inside a nested function?
questions.code:
def outer():
    total = 0
    def inner():
        nonlocal total
        total += 1
    inner()
    return total
choices: It reaches all the way to module-level (global) scope
It lets `inner` reassign a variable from the nearest enclosing function scope, rather than creating a new local
It is a synonym for `global`
It makes `total` read-only inside `inner`

query.title: The nonlocal keyword
query.explanation: Without `nonlocal`, assigning to `total` inside `inner` would create a brand-new local variable in `inner`’s own scope, shadowing the outer one instead of modifying it, the same problem `global` solves one level further out. `nonlocal` specifically targets the nearest enclosing function scope (not the module scope), which is what closures over mutable counters rely on.

questions.prompt: `"hello".encode("utf-8")` returns a `str` object, the same type it started as.

query.title: str.encode() and bytes.decode()
query.explanation: A Python `str` is a sequence of abstract Unicode code points with no inherent byte layout. `.encode(encoding)` converts it to a concrete `bytes` object using a specific encoding scheme like UTF-8, and `.decode(encoding)` does the reverse, turning raw bytes back into text; using the wrong encoding on decode can raise `UnicodeDecodeError` or silently produce garbled text.

questions.prompt: Why does `a = 1000; b = 1000; a is b` commonly print `False` even though `a == b` is `True`?
questions.code:
a = 1000
b = 1000
print(a == b, a is b)
choices: `==` and `is` always agree for integers, this is a trick question
`==` compares values; `is` compares object identity, and large integers outside the small-int cache are typically separate objects
`is` is deprecated and always returns `False`
`1000` is not a valid integer literal

query.title: is vs ==
query.syntax:
a == b   # value equality, calls __eq__
a is b   # identity, same object in memory
query.explanation: `==` invokes `__eq__` to compare values according to whatever equality the type defines. `is` instead checks whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory. Small integers may be cached and shared, but larger ones like `1000` are ordinarily allocated separately each time, so relying on `is` for value comparison of arbitrary integers is a bug waiting to happen.

questions.prompt: A tuple like `(1, 2)` can be used as a dictionary key, but a list like `[1, 2]` cannot.

query.title: Hashability and dict keys
query.syntax:
d = {(1, 2): 'pair'}   # OK
d = {[1, 2]: 'pair'}   # TypeError: unhashable type
query.explanation: Dict keys must be hashable, meaning their hash value cannot change over their lifetime, which requires immutability. Tuples are immutable and hashable (as long as everything inside them is also hashable), while lists are mutable and therefore explicitly excluded from hashing, raising `TypeError` if you try to use one as a key.

questions.prompt: Given `def f(a, b, c): ...`, which of these calls is invalid?
choices: f(1, a=1, b=2, c=3)  — raises TypeError for a duplicate value for argument "a"
f(1, c=3, b=2)  — raises TypeError
f(a=1, b=2, c=3)  — raises TypeError
Neither call is invalid

query.title: Mixing positional and keyword arguments
query.syntax: f(pos1, pos2, kw=value)   # positional args must come before keyword args
query.explanation: Positional arguments fill parameters left to right, and any parameter already filled positionally cannot also be supplied by keyword; Python raises `TypeError: got multiple values for argument`. Here the leading `1` already fills `a`, so also passing `a=1` by keyword collides with it, even though the value is identical.

questions.prompt: How does Python evaluate the chained comparison `1 < x < 10`?
choices: As `(1 < x) < 10`, comparing a boolean to `10`
As `1 < x and x < 10`, with `x` evaluated only once
It is a SyntaxError, comparisons cannot be chained
As `1 < x or x < 10`

query.title: Chained comparisons
query.syntax: a < b < c   ==   (a < b) and (b < c), but b evaluated once
query.explanation: Python treats a chain of comparison operators as an implicit `and` of each adjacent pair, short-circuiting the moment one comparison is false. Unlike manually writing `(1 < x) < 10`, which would compare a `bool` to `10`, chaining evaluates the middle expression `x` only once and applies both comparisons directly to it.

questions.prompt: The conditional expression `"even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"` evaluates only the branch selected by the condition, never both branches.

query.title: Conditional (ternary) expressions
query.explanation: Python’s conditional expression evaluates the condition first, and depending on its truthiness, returns one of the two branch expressions as the overall value of the expression. It is not a statement, unlike an `if`/`else` block, so it can be embedded directly inside an assignment, a function call, or a list comprehension.

questions.prompt: After `a = b = []`, calling `a.append(1)` also makes `b` equal to `[1]`, because both names refer to the same list object.

query.title: Chained assignment shares one object
query.syntax: a = b = mutable_expression()   # both names bind to the SAME object
query.explanation: A chained assignment like `a = b = []` evaluates the right-hand side exactly once and binds every target name to that single resulting object; it does not create two separate empty lists. Since lists are mutable, mutating through either name is visible through the other, which is different from writing `a = []` and `b = []` on separate lines.

questions.prompt: What is the idiomatic way to swap two variables in Python?
questions.code:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
choices: Using a temporary variable, since Python has no other way
Tuple packing and unpacking in one line: `a, b = b, a`
Calling `swap(a, b)`, a built-in function
It is not possible without the `copy` module

query.title: Swapping via tuple unpacking
query.explanation: The right-hand side `b, a` is first packed into a temporary tuple in its original order, and only then is that tuple unpacked into `a` and `b` on the left. Because the whole right side is evaluated before any assignment happens, there is no need for a manual temporary variable to avoid overwriting a value too early.

questions.prompt: `'ab' * 3` evaluates to `'ababab'`.

query.title: String repetition with *
query.syntax: sequence * n   # repeats the sequence n times
query.explanation: The `*` operator on a string (or any sequence) with an integer repeats the entire sequence that many times and concatenates the copies, producing a new string rather than mutating anything. It is a convenient shorthand for building a padded or repeated string without a loop or `str.join`.

questions.prompt: Writing `rows = [[0] * 3] * 3` to build a 3x3 grid means mutating one inner list, e.g. `rows[0][0] = 1`, will also change the corresponding entry in every other row.

query.title: List multiplication aliases inner mutable objects
query.syntax: [[0] * n] * m   # WRONG for a mutable grid, all rows are the same list
query.explanation: The outer `* 3` does not create three independent inner lists; it copies the same reference to one inner list three times, the same aliasing behavior as `a = b = []`. Mutating that shared inner list through any row name is visible through all of them. The correct idiom is `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`, which creates a fresh list on each comprehension iteration.

questions.prompt: What does `all([1, 2, 0, 4])` return, and why?
choices: True, because the list is non-empty
False, because 0 is falsy and all() requires every element to be truthy
True, because most elements are truthy
It raises TypeError on a list containing 0

query.title: all() and any()
query.syntax:
all(iterable)   # True if every element is truthy (or empty)
any(iterable)   # True if at least one element is truthy
query.explanation: `all()` short-circuits and returns `False` as soon as it finds one falsy element; `0` is falsy, so the whole call is `False` regardless of the other truthy elements. `all([])` on an empty iterable returns `True` (vacuous truth), the mirror opposite of `any([])`, which returns `False`.

questions.prompt: What does `map(str.upper, ["a", "b"])` return, before you do anything else with it?
choices: ['A', 'B'], a list
A `map` object, a lazy iterator; nothing is computed until it's consumed
'AB', a single string
A TypeError, map needs a lambda, not a bound method

query.title: map() is lazy
query.explanation: Like `range` and generator expressions, `map` in Python 3 returns a lazy iterator object rather than eagerly building a list, so `str.upper` has not actually been called on anything yet at the point `result` is created. You need `list(result)` or a `for` loop to force evaluation and get concrete values out.

questions.prompt: What does `list(filter(None, [0, 1, "", "a", None, 2]))` produce?
choices: A TypeError, `None` is not callable

query.title: filter() with None as the predicate
query.syntax: filter(None, iterable)   # keeps only truthy elements
query.explanation: Passing `None` instead of a function to `filter` is a documented special case meaning "use truthiness itself as the test." Every falsy element, `0`, `""`, and `None` here, is dropped, and every truthy element is kept, which is a quick way to strip a mix of empty/falsy values out of an iterable.

questions.prompt: Why does `sorted(names, key=lambda: n.lower())` fail to run at all?
choices: lambdas cannot reference variables at all
The lambda takes zero parameters, but `sorted` calls the key function with one argument (each element)
`lower()` does not exist on strings
lambdas cannot be passed as arguments to other functions

query.title: lambda expression syntax
query.explanation: A `lambda` is an anonymous function restricted to a single expression body, but it still declares its own parameter list like any function. `sorted` calls the `key` function once per element, passing that element as one positional argument; a zero-parameter lambda like `lambda: n.lower()` cannot accept that argument and raises `TypeError`. It should read `lambda n: n.lower()`.

questions.prompt: Calling `config.get("timeout", 30)` raises `KeyError` if `"timeout"` is not a key in `config`.

query.title: dict.get(key, default)
query.explanation: Unlike `config["timeout"]`, which raises `KeyError` on a missing key, `.get` returns the given default (or `None` if no default is supplied) and never mutates the dict. This is the common pattern for reading optional configuration values without wrapping every access in a `try`/`except`.

questions.prompt: What does `groups.setdefault("a", []).append(1)` do if `"a"` is not yet a key in `groups`?
choices: Raises `KeyError` because `"a"` does not exist yet
Inserts `"a": []` into `groups`, then appends `1` to that new list, leaving `groups == {"a": [1]}`
Does nothing, since `setdefault` only reads existing keys
Overwrites any existing value for `"a"` with `[1]`

query.title: dict.setdefault(key, default)
query.explanation: If the key is missing, `setdefault` inserts it with the given default value and returns that same value; if the key already exists, it leaves the dict untouched and returns the existing value instead. Chaining `.append(1)` onto the returned list is what makes this a common one-line alternative to `defaultdict` for ad-hoc grouping.

questions.prompt: What does `{"a": 1, "b": 2} | {"b": 3, "c": 4}` evaluate to (Python 3.9+)?
choices: A TypeError, dicts do not support `|`

query.title: Dict union with |
query.syntax: dict1 | dict2   # right operand wins on key conflicts
query.explanation: Python 3.9 added `|` as a merge operator for dicts, returning a new dict containing all keys from both operands. Where a key appears in both, the value from the right-hand dict wins, exactly like `{**dict1, **dict2}` did before this operator existed; neither original dict is modified.

questions.prompt: What does `{1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4}` return?
choices: set()

query.title: Set intersection operator
query.syntax:
set1 & set2   # intersection
set1 | set2   # union
set1 - set2   # difference
query.explanation: The `&` operator on two sets returns their intersection, the elements present in both. `|` returns the union of all unique elements from either set, and `-` returns the elements in the left set that are absent from the right. These map directly to `.intersection()`, `.union()`, and `.difference()` methods with identical semantics.

questions.prompt: A `frozenset` can be used as a dictionary key or stored inside another set, but a regular `set` cannot.

query.title: frozenset immutability
query.explanation: `frozenset` is an immutable variant of `set`: once created its contents cannot change, which makes it hashable the same way tuples are hashable but lists are not. A plain mutable `set` is unhashable for the same reason mutable containers generally are, so it cannot serve as a dict key or live inside another set.

questions.prompt: After `s = "hello"; s.upper()`, what is `s`?
choices: 'HELLO', because .upper() mutates the string in place
'hello', unchanged, because strings are immutable and .upper() returns a new string
An error, strings have no `.upper()` method
'Hello'

query.title: Strings are immutable
query.syntax: new_s = s.upper()   # must capture the return value
query.explanation: Every string method that appears to "transform" a string, `.upper()`, `.strip()`, `.replace()`, and so on, actually returns a brand-new string and leaves the original object untouched. Because `str` has no mutating methods, forgetting to assign the result (`s = s.upper()`) is a common beginner-to-intermediate mistake that silently does nothing.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `lst.append(x)` and `lst.extend(x)` when `x` is itself a list?
choices: They are identical, just different names for the same operation
`append` adds `x` as a single new element (even if it is a list); `extend` iterates over `x` and adds each of its elements individually
`extend` only works on tuples, not lists
`append` raises `TypeError` if given a list

query.title: list.append vs list.extend
query.explanation: `append` always adds exactly one new element to the end of the list, whatever object you pass it, so appending a list nests it as a sublist. `extend` instead treats its argument as an iterable and adds each of its elements in turn, which is what you usually want when combining two flat lists.

questions.prompt: Calling `lst.pop(0)` on `[10, 20, 30]` removes and returns `10`, leaving the list as `[20, 30]`.

query.title: list.pop(index)
query.syntax:
lst.pop()        # removes and returns the LAST element
lst.pop(index)   # removes and returns the element at index
query.explanation: With no argument, `.pop()` removes and returns the last element, an O(1) operation. Passing an explicit index removes and returns the element at that position instead, shifting every later element down by one, which makes `.pop(0)` an O(n) operation on a list since the remaining elements have to move.

questions.prompt: Both `del lst[0]` and `lst.pop(0)` remove the first element of a list, but only `.pop(0)` returns the removed value.
questions.code:
lst = [1, 2, 3]
del lst[0]      # removes it, returns nothing

lst2 = [1, 2, 3]
x = lst2.pop(0)  # removes it, returns 1

query.title: del statement vs pop()
query.syntax:
del target        # unbinds/removes, no return value
obj.pop(key)      # removes AND returns the value
query.explanation: `del` is a statement, not a method call, and it works on list items, dict keys, slices, and even plain variable names (`del x` unbinds `x` entirely), but it never produces a usable return value. `.pop()` is specifically a method on lists and dicts that removes the target and hands back its value in one step, useful when you need the removed item.

questions.prompt: What does `lst = [1, 2, 3, 4]; lst[1:3] = [9]` leave `lst` as?
choices: A ValueError, the replacement must match the slice length

query.title: Slice assignment can change list length
query.explanation: Assigning to a slice replaces exactly the elements in that range with the elements of the right-hand iterable, and the two do not need to be the same length. Here the two-element slice `[2, 3]` is replaced by a one-element list, so the overall list shrinks by one, unlike assigning to a single index which requires no such length match.

questions.prompt: Calling `lst[-1]` on a non-empty list raises `IndexError`, since negative numbers are not valid indices.

query.title: Negative indexing
query.syntax:
sequence[-1]   # last element
sequence[-2]   # second to last
query.explanation: Negative indices count backward from the end of the sequence, with `-1` referring to the last element, `-2` to the second-to-last, and so on. It is equivalent to `lst[len(lst) - 1]` but avoids computing the length explicitly, and it works the same way for strings and tuples.

questions.prompt: `range(10_000_000)` allocates a list of ten million integers in memory as soon as it is created.

query.title: range() is lazy
query.syntax: range(start, stop, step)   # a lazy sequence object
query.explanation: A `range` object stores only its start, stop, and step values and computes each element on demand as it is iterated or indexed; it never materializes the full sequence in memory. This is why `range(10_000_000_000)` is created instantly with negligible memory, whereas `list(range(10_000_000_000))` would try to allocate all of it at once.

questions.prompt: What happens when you call `next()` on an exhausted iterator?
choices: It returns `None`
It raises `StopIteration`
It silently restarts from the beginning
It raises `IndexError`

query.title: Manual iterator protocol
query.syntax:
it = iter(iterable)
next(it)   # raises StopIteration when exhausted
query.explanation: `iter()` gets an iterator from an iterable, and repeated calls to `next()` pull successive values from it. Once there are no more values, `next()` raises `StopIteration` rather than returning a sentinel like `None`, which matters because `0`, `""`, or `None` could all be legitimate yielded values; a `for` loop catches this exception internally to know when to stop.

questions.prompt: When does the `else` clause of a `try`/`except`/`else` block run?
choices: Only if an exception was caught
Only if the `try` block completed with no exception raised
Always, regardless of whether an exception occurred
Only if there is no `except` clause at all

query.title: try/except/else
query.explanation: The `else` clause on a `try` statement runs only when the `try` block finished without raising, which lets you separate "code that might fail" from "code that should only run on success" without accidentally catching exceptions raised by the success-path code itself. `finally`, by contrast, runs unconditionally, whether or not an exception occurred or was caught.

questions.prompt: What does `except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:` do?
choices: It is a syntax error; each exception type needs its own `except` clause
It catches either a `ValueError` or a `TypeError` with one clause, binding whichever was raised to `e`
It only catches `ValueError`, the tuple is ignored
It catches only exceptions that are simultaneously both types

query.title: Catching multiple exception types
query.explanation: Parentheses after `except` let you list several exception types that should be handled the same way; Python catches the first one raised that matches any type in the tuple and binds it to `e`. This avoids duplicating the same handler body across multiple separate `except` clauses when the recovery logic is identical.

questions.prompt: What does a bare `raise` (with no exception given) do inside an `except` block?
choices: Raises a generic `Exception`
Re-raises the exception currently being handled, preserving its original traceback
Does nothing, it is a no-op outside a function
Raises `StopIteration`

query.title: Bare raise re-raises the active exception
query.explanation: Inside an `except` block, `raise` with no arguments looks up the exception currently being handled and raises that exact same exception object again, keeping its original traceback intact. This is the standard way to log or react to an exception and then let it continue propagating, rather than swallowing it.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of `pathlib.Path` over building paths with `os.path` and string concatenation?
questions.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("data") / "raw" / "file.csv"
choices: It is the only way to check if a file exists
The `/` operator joins path segments in an object-oriented way, and it is OS-independent about separators
`os.path` is deprecated and no longer works
`pathlib.Path` objects can be used interchangeably with integers

query.title: pathlib.Path
query.explanation: `pathlib` overloads the `/` operator on `Path` objects so joining directory segments reads naturally left to right, and it automatically uses the correct separator for the current operating system instead of hardcoded forward or back slashes. It also bundles common operations like `.exists()`, `.read_text()`, and `.suffix` directly as methods and properties on the path object.

questions.prompt: What does `json.dumps({"a": 1, "b": [1, 2]})` return?
choices: A JSON-formatted string: '{"a": 1, "b": [1, 2]}'
A bytes object
Writes directly to a file named after the dict

query.title: json.dumps / json.loads
query.explanation: `json.dumps` serializes a Python object built from JSON-compatible types (dict, list, str, int, float, bool, None) into a JSON-formatted string. `json.loads` performs the inverse operation, parsing a JSON string back into the equivalent Python objects; `dump`/`load` (no "s") do the same thing directly against a file object instead of returning/accepting a string.

questions.prompt: What does `datetime(2024, 1, 31) + timedelta(days=1)` evaluate to?
questions.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
datetime(2024, 1, 31) + timedelta(days=1)
choices: datetime(2024, 1, 32)
datetime(2024, 2, 1)
A ValueError, January has only 31 days
datetime(2024, 1, 30)

query.title: datetime + timedelta arithmetic
query.explanation: `timedelta` represents a duration, and adding one to a `datetime` correctly rolls over month and year boundaries rather than just incrementing the day field naively, which is exactly why `datetime` objects overload `+` and `-` instead of leaving date arithmetic to manual field manipulation. The result here correctly lands on February 1st.

questions.prompt: What does calling `random.seed(42)` before generating random numbers accomplish?
choices: It makes every future call to `random.random()` return exactly `42`
It initializes the pseudo-random generator so the resulting sequence of "random" numbers is reproducible
It disables randomness, making the module raise an error on use
It only affects `random.randint`, not other functions in the module

query.title: random.seed()
query.explanation: Python’s `random` module produces pseudo-random numbers from a deterministic algorithm driven by internal state. Calling `.seed(42)` resets that internal state to a fixed, known point, so every subsequent call to `random()`, `randint()`, `choice()`, and so on produces the exact same sequence every time the program runs, which is essential for reproducible tests and simulations.

questions.prompt: Calling `.strip()` with no arguments on `"  hi there  "` removes whitespace only from the start and end, leaving the internal space between "hi" and "there" intact.

query.title: str.strip() default behavior
query.syntax:
str.strip()          # removes leading/trailing whitespace
str.strip(chars)     # removes leading/trailing chars in the given set
query.explanation: With no argument, `.strip()` removes whitespace characters (spaces, tabs, newlines) only from the very start and end of the string, leaving whitespace in the middle untouched. It is distinct from `.split()`, which by default splits on any run of whitespace anywhere in the string and returns a list of the resulting pieces.

questions.prompt: What does `"report.csv".endswith((".csv", ".tsv"))` return?
choices: A TypeError, endswith only accepts a single string
True, because a tuple of suffixes checks if any of them match
False, because the argument is a tuple, not a string
'.csv'

query.title: startswith()/endswith() accept a tuple
query.explanation: Both `.startswith()` and `.endswith()` accept either a single string or a tuple of strings as their argument. When given a tuple, they return `True` if the string matches any one of the entries, which avoids writing `s.endswith(".csv") or s.endswith(".tsv")` by hand.

questions.prompt: For a dict `d`, the expression `"x" in d` checks whether `"x"` is one of the dict’s keys, not whether it is one of the values.

query.title: in operator on dicts checks keys
query.syntax:
key in dict          # checks keys
value in dict.values()  # checks values
query.explanation: Iterating over a dict directly, whether with `in`, a `for` loop, or `list(d)`, walks its keys, not its key-value pairs or values. To test membership among the values instead, you must explicitly write `value in d.values()`, which is an O(n) scan, unlike key lookups which are O(1) average case.

questions.prompt: Why does `len(my_custom_object)` work for a user-defined class with no inheritance from any built-in container?
choices: It does not work, `len()` only works on built-in types
Python's `len()` calls the object's `__len__` method; any class defining it works, regardless of inheritance
The class must inherit from `list` for `len()` to work
`len()` silently returns 0 for any object without a length

query.title: Duck typing via __len__
query.explanation: The built-in `len()` function does not check the object’s class hierarchy; it simply calls `__len__()` on whatever object it is given and returns the result. This is Python’s duck typing in action: any object that implements the right dunder methods can participate in the corresponding built-in protocol, no matter what it inherits from.

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to instantiate a class that inherits from `abc.ABC` but has not implemented one of its `@abstractmethod` methods?
choices: It works fine, abstract methods are just documentation
Python raises `TypeError` at instantiation time, refusing to create the object
It creates the object but calling `.area()` raises `NotImplementedError`
It silently returns `None` instead of an instance

query.title: abc.ABC and @abstractmethod
query.explanation: Unlike a method body that just raises `NotImplementedError`, marking a method `@abstractmethod` on a class deriving from `ABC` is enforced by the metaclass machinery: attempting to instantiate any subclass that has not overridden every abstract method raises `TypeError` immediately, before any of its code runs, catching the mistake much earlier.

questions.prompt: Reassigning a class attribute through one instance, like `instance.shared = 5`, changes the value for every other instance of that class too.

query.title: Class attributes vs instance attributes
query.syntax:
class C:
    shared = 0   # class attribute, shared until shadowed

c = C()
c.shared = 5   # creates an INSTANCE attribute, does not touch C.shared
query.explanation: Reading `instance.shared` falls back to the class attribute only if the instance has no attribute of that name itself. Assigning `instance.shared = 5` does not mutate the class attribute; it creates a brand-new instance attribute on that one object that shadows the class attribute for lookups through that instance only, leaving `C.shared` and every other instance unaffected.

questions.prompt: What does calling `super().__init__(name)` inside a subclass’s `__init__` do?
choices: Creates a brand-new, unrelated `Animal` instance and discards it
Calls the parent class's `__init__` on the current instance, letting the subclass reuse the parent's setup logic
Is only valid syntax inside `__init__`, never in other methods
Skips the parent class entirely and calls `object.__init__` directly

query.title: super() in __init__
query.explanation: `super()` returns a proxy that dispatches method calls to the next class in the current instance’s MRO, most commonly the immediate parent. Calling `super().__init__(name)` runs the parent’s initialization logic against `self`, letting the subclass extend rather than duplicate it, which is why `self.name` ends up set even though `Dog.__init__` never assigns it directly.

questions.prompt: Given `data = (1, (2, 3), 4)`, what does `a, (b, c), d = data` bind `b` and `c` to?
choices: b=(2, 3), c=undefined
A ValueError, nested unpacking is not allowed

query.title: Nested unpacking
query.explanation: Unpacking targets can themselves be parenthesized tuples (or lists), which recursively unpack the corresponding nested element of the right-hand side. Here the middle target `(b, c)` matches against the middle element `(2, 3)` of the same shape, binding `b` and `c` to its two elements individually rather than binding one name to the whole sub-tuple.

questions.prompt: What makes this method chaining pattern work, `builder.add(1).add(2).build()`?
choices: Python automatically chains methods on any class
Each method explicitly returns `self`, so the next `.method()` call is made on the same instance
`add` must be a `@staticmethod` for chaining to work
Chaining only works with built-in types like strings

query.title: Method chaining via returning self
query.explanation: There is no special language feature for method chaining; it works purely because each method explicitly `return self`, handing back the same instance so the next dotted call in the expression has something to operate on. If `add` forgot the `return self`, the chain would break with `AttributeError: NoneType has no attribute add`.

questions.prompt: What does `[x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]` produce?
questions.code: [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
choices: [True, False, True, ...]

query.title: Comprehension with a filter clause
query.syntax: [expr for target in iterable if condition]
query.explanation: The trailing `if` clause in a comprehension acts purely as a filter: for each item produced by the `for` clause, Python evaluates the condition and only computes and includes `expr` in the result when it is true. Items that fail the condition are skipped entirely, never appearing in the output at all.

questions.prompt: What does `["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in range(4)]` produce?
questions.code: ["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in range(4)]
choices: ['even', 'odd']
['even', 'odd', 'even', 'odd']
A SyntaxError, if/else cannot appear before the for clause
['odd', 'even', 'odd', 'even']

query.title: Conditional expression inside a comprehension
query.syntax: [value_a if condition else value_b for target in iterable]
query.explanation: This is different from the filtering `if` that trails a comprehension: placed immediately after the output expression and before the `for` clause, `if`/`else` forms a ternary conditional expression that Python evaluates for every single item, choosing between two output values rather than deciding whether to include the item at all.

questions.prompt: What does `[x for row in matrix for x in row]` do for `matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]`?
questions.code:
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
[x for row in matrix for x in row]
choices: A SyntaxError, comprehensions allow only one for clause

query.title: Nested (flattening) comprehension
query.syntax: [expr for outer in outer_iterable for inner in outer]
query.explanation: A comprehension can chain multiple `for` clauses, which nest exactly like stacked `for` loops written left to right: the leftmost is the outer loop and each subsequent one is nested inside it. Here the outer loop walks each row and the inner loop walks each element of that row, flattening the 2D structure into a single flat list.

questions.prompt: What does `functools.reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [1, 2, 3, 4], 0)` compute?
questions.code:
from functools import reduce
reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [1, 2, 3, 4], 0)
choices: A TypeError, reduce needs exactly two arguments

query.title: functools.reduce
query.explanation: `reduce` repeatedly applies a two-argument function to an accumulator and the next item of the iterable, folding the whole sequence down to one value. Starting from the initializer `0`, it computes `0+1=1`, then `1+2=3`, then `3+3=6`, then `6+4=10`, ending at `10`; omitting the initializer would instead use the iterable’s first element as the starting accumulator.

questions.prompt: What does `functools.partial(pow, exp=2)` produce?
questions.code:
from functools import partial
square = partial(pow, exp=2)
square(base=5)
choices: A number, `25`, computed immediately
A new callable with `exp` pre-filled to `2`, so calling it only needs the remaining arguments
A `TypeError`, partial cannot be used with keyword arguments
An identical copy of the `pow` function

query.title: functools.partial
query.explanation: `partial` does not call the function; it returns a new callable that remembers some arguments as already filled in, and merges them with whatever arguments are supplied at the eventual call site. This is a lightweight alternative to writing a small wrapper function or lambda just to pin down a few parameters.

questions.prompt: What does `list(zip(*[(1, "a"), (2, "b"), (3, "c")]))` produce?
choices: A TypeError, zip cannot be unpacked with *

query.title: zip(*pairs) as an unzip idiom
query.explanation: Unpacking the list of tuples with `*` passes each tuple as a separate positional argument to `zip`, which then groups the first elements of every argument together, then the second elements, and so on. Applied to a list of pairs, this transposes rows into columns, which is why `zip(*...)` is the standard idiom for "unzipping" a list of tuples.

questions.prompt: The old-style `%` string formatting operator, as in `'%s scored %d' % ('Sam', 9)`, substitutes values positionally into the string, similar in spirit to `str.format()` or f-strings.

query.title: Old-style % string formatting
query.explanation: The `%` operator on a string is the original, printf-style formatting mechanism: `%s` substitutes a value via `str()`, `%d` substitutes an integer, and so on, matched positionally against a tuple on the right-hand side. It predates both `str.format()` and f-strings and still appears in older codebases and some logging call sites.

questions.prompt: Writing `return a, b` inside a function returns a tuple `(a, b)`, which the caller can unpack directly with `x, y = f()`.

query.title: Returning multiple values as a tuple
query.explanation: Python has no dedicated "multiple return value" mechanism; `return a, b` is just returning one object, a tuple built from packing `a` and `b` together via the same comma syntax used elsewhere. The caller then unpacks that single tuple into separate names, which is why parentheses around the returned values are optional but unpacking on the receiving end is required to get individual variables back out.

questions.prompt: What does the bare `*` do in this function signature?
questions.code:
def connect(host, port, *, timeout=30):
    ...

connect("localhost", 8080, timeout=5)   # OK
connect("localhost", 8080, 5)            # TypeError
choices: It collects extra positional arguments, just like `*args`
It marks every parameter after it as keyword-only, callers cannot pass them positionally
It is a syntax error on its own with no name attached
It makes `timeout` a required positional argument

query.title: Keyword-only arguments with a bare *
query.explanation: A lone `*` in a parameter list, with no name attached, does not collect anything itself; it is purely a marker that ends the positional parameter section. Every parameter listed after it can only be supplied by keyword, which is why `connect("localhost", 8080, 5)` fails, `5` cannot be matched to `timeout` positionally, forcing callers to write `timeout=5` explicitly and improving call-site clarity.
